**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5658442, Reactome:R-HSA-6802953)

**Proposed mechanism:** NF1 (HGNC:7779) —DISRUPTS→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP401); RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP401) —LEADS_TO→ Neurofibromatosis type 1 (MONDO:0018975); NRAS (HGNC:7929) —DISRUPTS→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP401); HRAS (HGNC:4837) —DISRUPTS→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP401); RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP401) —LEADS_TO→ Thyroid cancer, nonmedullary, 2 (MONDO:0008566). Loss of function of NF1 leads to dysregulation of the RAS signaling pathway, contributing to the phenotypes of neurofibromatosis type 1. Concurrently, gain-of-function mutations in RAS family genes (NRAS, HRAS) also dysregulate the same RAS signaling pathway, driving the development of nonmedullary thyroid cancer type 2. The convergence occurs at the level of the RAS signaling pathway, a central node in cellular proliferation and differentiation.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that the RAS signaling pathway is not affected by mutations in NF1 or that mutations in NRAS/HRAS do not impact this pathway in the context of thyroid cancer. _(variant: gnomad v2.1.1 shows pathogenic variants in NF1, NRAS, and HRAS with low allele frequencies (<0.001%) in relevant populations, consistent with rare disease causality.)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the RAS signaling pathway, which is implicated in both diseases, could offer therapeutic strategies for both neurofibromatosis type 1 and nonmedullary thyroid cancer, potentially through MEK inhibitors or other pathway modulators.

#### 10. urinary bladder cancer  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.395)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5658442, Reactome:R-HSA-6802953)

**Proposed mechanism:** NF1 (HGNC:7772) —DECREASES→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400); RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400) —LEADS_TO→ Neurofibromas (HP:0000981); HRAS (HGNC:4835) —INCREASES→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400); KRAS (HGNC:6407) —INCREASES→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400); FGFR3 (HGNC:3137) —INCREASES→ RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400); RAS signaling pathway (WP:WP400) —LEADS_TO→ Urinary bladder cancer (MONDO:0001187). Loss of function of NF1 leads to dysregulation of the RAS signaling pathway, contributing to neurofibroma formation. Conversely, gain-of-function mutations in HRAS, KRAS, or FGFR3 (which can signal through RAS) promote constitutive activation of the RAS pathway, driving the development of urinary bladder cancer. The shared convergence on the RAS signaling pathway represents the mechanistic link.

**How to falsify it:** If mutations in NF1 were found to exclusively promote a gain-of-function phenotype or if mutations in HRAS, KRAS, and FGFR3 did not activate the RAS signaling pathway in bladder cancer, this hypothesis would be falsified. Additionally, if genetic studies show no significant overlap in the RAS pathway's role between these two conditions. _(variant: Common variants (>1% allele frequency) in NF1, HRAS, KRAS, or FGFR3 that are established to cause loss-of-function in NF1 or gain-of-function in bladder cancer, respectively.)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the RAS signaling pathway could offer therapeutic strategies for both NF1-associated plexiform neurofibromas and urinary bladder cancer, potentially through MEK or ERK inhibitors, or by modulating upstream regulators.
